records.title: From digital diplomacy to AI-driven diplomacies? Mapping the potential impact of AI on Diplomacy
records.abstract: The rapid and consecutive launch of artificial intelligence applications over the past 3 years has led digital diplomacy scholars to envision the future of artificial intelligence–driven diplomacy. This article argues that while such visions are enthralling, they are also highly speculative. To better examine how artificial intelligence may impact diplomacy, this article employs an extensive analysis of digital diplomacy scholarship. By analyzing digital diplomacy studies published over the past 12 years, this article identifies the societal, institutional, and economic factors that ultimately shape how diplomats employ digital technologies. This article suggests that these factors may lead to three scenarios of artificial intelligence–driven diplomacies: a “De-evolution scenario,” in which diplomats are reduced to data gatherers, an “Augmentation scenario,” where artificial intelligence insight enables diplomats to better manage crises, and a “Virtuality scenario,” where artificial intelligence and virtual reality facilitate interpersonal communication and negotiations between diplomats. This article also outlines two inherent paradoxes that may limit the use of artificial intelligence in diplomacy: a temporal paradox and an uncertainty paradox. Through these three scenarios and two paradoxes, this article illustrates the contours of artificial intelligence–driven diplomacy.

records.title: Can Responsible AI Exist Without Responsible Institutions? An Institutional Responsibility Framework for AI Governance
records.abstract: The rapid diffusion of artificial intelligence (AI) has transformed governance from a predominantly technical challenge into a normative and institutional one. Although the Responsible AI literature has established widely accepted ethical principles including fairness, accountability, transparency, explainability, and human oversight, it has devoted comparatively little attention to the institutions responsible for translating these principles into legitimate governance. Existing scholarship largely treats institutions as mechanisms for implementing ethical commitments rather than as normative actors whose responsibility itself requires philosophical justification. This article addresses that conceptual gap by asking: Can Responsible AI exist without Responsible Institutions? Using a philosophical and interdisciplinary conceptual analysis, it draws on Responsible AI scholarship, institutional theory, public administration, political philosophy, and digital government to develop Institutional Responsibility as a distinct normative concept and proposes the Institutional Responsibility Framework (IRF) as its principal theoretical contribution. The framework conceptualises responsibility as institutionally constituted, distributed, exercised, justified, and sustained across complex AI governance ecosystems. It argues that Responsible AI presupposes responsible institutions because ethical principles cannot govern AI independently of the institutional arrangements that establish legitimate authority, coordinate governance, and sustain public trust. records.title: Hybrid Governance Framework: Governing Human-AI Decision Authority in AI-Enabled Decision Systems
records.abstract: Artificial intelligence is increasingly embedded in organizational decision infrastructures, shaping how firms generate insights, allocate resources, and execute strategic actions. In marketing environments, these systems influence decisions through algorithmic recommendations, automated optimization, and real-time analytics. While prior research has examined marketing analytics, AI augmentation, and hybrid intelligence architectures, significantly less attention has been devoted to how these hybrid systems should be governed. Existing governance models were largely developed for human managerial decision environments and do not fully account for algorithmic agency, recursive learning, and automated decision execution. This article develops a conceptual framework termed the Hybrid Governance Framework (HGF) that explains how governance mechanisms structure and regulate decision authority across human and algorithmic actors in contemporary marketing systems. By positioning governance as an embedded architectural component of AI-enabled decision infrastructures, the framework clarifies how organizations can design stable hybrid decision systems that combine algorithmic intelligence with managerial oversight. The framework identifies three governance layers-algorithmic transparency, human oversight, and institutional control-that together stabilize hybrid decision environments. records.title: Authority and Responsibility Allocation in Human–AI Collaborative Decision-Making: Governance Mechanisms for Enterprises
records.abstract: Artificial intelligence is moving from analytical support toward active participation in enterprise decisions, creating an organization-design problem: firms must decide which rights may be delegated to AI and how responsibility should follow the actors who can prevent, challenge, or remedy failure. Existing work explains automation, augmentation, delegation, human oversight, and responsible AI governance, but does not reveal how specific transfers of decision authority create responsibility gaps inside a focal enterprise decision. This conceptual paper develops a contingency governance framework through a transparent theory-synthesis procedure. A purposive corpus of 44 peer-reviewed studies, standards, and regulatory sources was assembled through anchor studies, targeted keyword searches, and citation chaining. First-order authority and responsibility terms were coded, compared, and abstracted until two successive search iterations produced no new categories. The resulting framework distinguishes seven decision rights—information access, recommendation, selection, approval, veto, execution, and escalation—and five responsibility domains—system design, decision process, outcome stewardship, oversight, and remediation. Its central mechanism is rights-control-responsibility alignment: delegating a right shifts effective control and evidence access, while governance fails when the responsible actor lacks the competence, authority, or information to intervene. records.title: (Mis)Understandings of defence diplomacy as public diplomacy: Insights from three Spanish elites
records.abstract: Defence diplomacy and public diplomacy are two diplomatic practices often treated in the literature as two disconnected realms. While the former focuses on the peaceful and cooperative use of armed forces, the latter emphasizes on the advancement of strategic communication in the international policy of actors. However, it is possible to bridge the differences between the two using the concept of soft power. By doing so, defence public diplomacy can be understood as a set of practices developed by states seeking to influence and attract third states while employing military force within these parameters. This paper contributes firstly to the conceptual debate bridging both types of diplomacies. Secondly, it selects a case study, Spain, to examine the perceptions of three different Spanish elites involved in the formulation and implementation of defence public policy: politicians, the military and defence industry managers. This paper adopts a qualitative methodology, including in-depth interviews, focus groups with experts, and manual content analysis of primary documentary sources. The results show that these elites agree on the importance of defence diplomacy for the achievement of state goals but continue to understand it fundamentally from a classical diplomatic prism. They also discuss the inclusion of new concepts, such as deterrence, as part of a defence public diplomacy.

records.title: A Study on Filipino Protocol Officers in Diplomatic Ceremonial Events
records.abstract: This study explored the roles and challenges encountered by Filipino Protocol Officers in managing diplomatic ceremonial events. These officers played a vital role in ensuring the seamless execution of formal state functions and diplomatic interactions, balancing respect for tradition with the evolving demands of modern diplomacy. Using qualitative methods, including semi-structured interviews and document analysis, the research examined the officers’ preparation strategies, adherence to established protocol, and navigation of cultural nuances. Key findings underscored the critical importance of meticulous planning, cultural sensitivity, and effective inter-agency coordination. The study also identified major challenges, such as communication gaps, conflicting customs, and workload-related stress, along with the strategies employed to address them. Overall, this study contributed to a deeper understanding of the complexities involved in diplomatic protocol and offered recommendations for improving ceremonial event management practices in the Philippines.

records.title: Regionalism as Diplomacy
records.abstract: This chapter explains why two consensus-based Asian regional organizations have produced sharply different records in security governance. It argues that ASEAN scales security cooperation not through supranational authority, but through the steady accumulation of diplomatic infrastructure, dense meeting routines, and layered fora that translate sovereignty sensitivity into managed informality and practical coordination. By contrast, SAARC's institutional design embeds high veto points and a constitutive rule excluding bilateral and contentious issues, which, when paired with persistent strategic rivalry, narrows the space of possible diplomacy and prevents security initiatives from being routinized. Using founding charters, key treaties, and institutional practice, the chapter shows how regionalism functions as diplomacy, shaping agendas, producing norms, and structuring crisis response. The concluding section draws implications for Asian order in an era of Indo-Pacific contestation and hybrid threats.

records.title: Managing the Crisis, Owning the Narrative: United States Diplomacy in the 2025 India–Pakistan Standoff
records.abstract: The 2025 terrorist attack in Pahalgam, Kashmir, killed 26 civilians, raising India-Pakistan military tensions. In the days that followed, the US quickly engaged both sides diplomatically. The truce made Washington the crisis mediator. This article tests that claim. Did US crisis diplomacy advance strategic goals? Was it meant to demonstrate its importance and global dominance? This perspective documents historical events to address these questions. It contrasts diplomatic statements with media coverage. From there, it splits. Strategic diplomacy requires leverage, crisis management, and power, which are essential for negotiating favorable outcomes and maintaining international relations during conflicts. In contrast, symbolic diplomacy establishes credibility and communicates with multiple audiences. This pattern is clear from realist mediation and great-power context. Risk, notably nuclear escalation, alliance management in South Asia, and competitiveness with China motivated U.S. strategies, which generally emphasized regional stability and conflict prevention. The public story differed. Peace and temperance helped Washington appear steady and generous. The gap matters. Great powers are frequently interested, despite neutrality. Instead of competing, symbolic mediation and strategic calculation encouraged each other, allowing great countries to collaborate on global challenges. This confuses crisis management and global leadership.

records.abstract: Abstract This chapter focuses on the formal aspects of diplomatic relations. Meanwhile, the United Nations have orders of precedence between delegates and officials and between member countries. The chapter discusses the selections of heads of mission and the utilization of Full Power, which is a special authorization from the head of the State they represent.

It examines formal accountability requirements, operational instruments, public evidence, interviews with governance actors, and participatory validation to determine when accountability mechanisms influence institutional decisions and when they function primarily as procedural compliance. records.abstract: Artificial intelligence increasingly participates in the processes through which institutions interpret information, evaluate evidence, generate recommendations, make decisions, and act. Existing research and governance frameworks address AI risk management, human oversight, appropriate reliance, accountability, decision governance, and increasingly autonomous systems. A broader question nevertheless arises: how should institutions govern consequential judgment when the capabilities contributing to decisions and actions are distributed across human and artificial participants? This article advances Institutional Judgment Governance (IJG) as an integrative theoretical framework for examining that problem. IJG is defined as the governance of how institutions form, exercise, distribute, authorize, and evaluate consequential judgment; preserve the capacities required for such judgment; and remain accountable when human and artificial capabilities jointly contribute to organizational decision-making and action. It treats consequential institutional judgment as an institutionally attributable object of governance connecting AI capability with reliance, decision authority, delegated authority, judgment capacity, organizational action, and continuing accountability. records.title: Deterministic Decision Authority: A Governance-First Architecture for Human-Final AI Systems
records.abstract: Artificial intelligence systems increasingly participate in high-impact decision processes, yet most existing architectures lack a deterministic answer to a fundamental question: <em>who ultimately holds decision authority</em>. This paper introduces <strong>Deterministic Decision Authority (DDA)</strong>, a governance-first architectural framework designed to enforce human-final authority over AI-assisted decisions through mathematically defined constraints, irreversibility controls, and deterministic decision replay. Unlike conventional AI governance approaches that rely on post-hoc explainability or probabilistic alignment, DDA establishes decision authorization as a formally bounded process, separating intelligence generation from decision approval. The architecture integrates a non-modifiable decision core, a human-final governance layer, auto-lock mechanisms under uncertainty or irreversibility, and court-admissible audit traces. By design, the system cannot execute, optimize, or act autonomously, functioning instead as a deterministic decision authorization infrastructure. This work positions DDA as a distinct engineering and scientific discipline at the intersection of decision science, governance engineering, and applied mathematics, offering a scalable foundation for regulatory-grade AI deployment in high-risk domains such as finance, healthcare, and public policy.

records.title: Precedence Among Heads of Mission
records.abstract: Abstract This chapter discusses Articles 16, 17, and 18 of the Vienna Convention on Diplomatic Relations. Article 16 states that, in accordance with Article 13, heads of diplomatic missions take precedence in their respective classes in the order of the date and time of taking up their functions. It also states that any alterations made in the credentials of a head of mission that does not involve the changing of class shall not affect precedence. Lastly, the Article states that it is not prejudiced regarding the precedence of the representative of the Holy See. Article 17 on the other hand states that Ministry for Foreign Affairs or other similar body shall be notified of the precedence of the diplomatic staff, while Article 18 expresses that the procedure to be observed between each respective State for the reception of heads of mission shall be uniform in respect of class.

records.title: Judicial Diplomacy in Refugee Protection Governance: The ECtHR between Crisis Management and Rights-Centred Adjudication
records.abstract: Abstract This article rethinks the European Court of Human Rights’ role in refugee protection by reading its asylum-related case law as acts of judicial diplomacy. Diplomacy here is not institutional outreach; it is the Court’s reasoning practice: how it frames facts, allocates responsibility, and signals the practical limits of discretion under crisis pressure. This article develops a two-axis framework: (i) anticipatory and crisis-responsive diplomacy, capturing how Strasbourg calibrates tone, scope and evidentiary demands in high-stakes cases and (ii) vertical and horizontal diplomacy, tracking how judgments speak “downwards” into domestic asylum systems and “sideways” across overlapping legal regimes. A close reading of leading decisions on non-refoulement, jurisdiction, and vulnerability shows that the Court’s protective and restrictive strands often follow recurring diplomatic logics rather than mere inconsistency. This article concludes with a rights-centred benchmark for judicial diplomacy: legitimacy in refugee protection turns on making non-refoulement and individualised assessment practically reachable through clear jurisdictional reasoning and effective remedies.

records.title: The Feasibility of Implementing Corporate Governance within the Framework of Sustainability in Agricultural Enterprises
records.abstract: Agricultural enterprises play a strategic role in ensuring food security, protecting natural resources, and sustaining rural livelihoods. However, the governance structures traditionally designed for large publicly listed corporations are often unsuitable for the diverse organizational characteristics of agricultural businesses. This study examines the feasibility of implementing corporate governance frameworks in agricultural enterprises from a sustainability perspective and proposes a governance model tailored to the sector's specific needs. Drawing on the theoretical foundations of agency theory, shareholder theory, and stewardship theory, the study evaluates governance challenges across three major organizational forms: family-owned farms, agricultural cooperatives, and agri-food companies. It argues that effective governance in agriculture must extend beyond financial performance to incorporate environmental stewardship, social responsibility, and long-term resilience. The analysis identifies key barriers to implementation, including limited governance awareness, resource constraints, regulatory gaps, and the heterogeneity of agricultural enterprises. Rather than advocating a uniform governance model, the study emphasizes the need for flexible and adaptive governance mechanisms that reflect differences in enterprise size, ownership structure, and institutional context. records.title: A governança social e a responsabilidade institucional: paradigmas jurídicos para o compliance em direitos humanos no setor corporativo
records.abstract: Contemporaneity imposes on organizations, whether public or private, a duty of conduct that transcends mere formal legality, requiring substantive adherence to principles of social governance and respect for human rights. This scientific article proposes an exhaustive and technical analysis of the intersection between Public Advocacy, Social Security Law, and Social Compliance, establishing a new theoretical framework for institutional responsibility. The methodology is based on a systematic and critical bibliographic review, correlating international treaties, Brazilian legislation, and corporate governance theories (ESG). The study is structured into seven high-density thematic axes, exploring everything from the historical evolution of social responsibility to the implementation of human rights risk matrices. It discusses how corporate education and the creation of compliance protocols act as vectors for liability mitigation and equity promotion. The results indicate that organizational sustainability depends on the integration of ethical practices into institutional culture. It is concluded that the modern lawyer must act as an architect of integrity systems, capable of harmonizing profit with social welfare.

records.title: EU Norms, Legal Approximation, and Policy Change in Türkiye's Security Governance
records.abstract: This study aims to analyze the impact of European Union (EU) norms on Türkiye's security policies. In this study, the transformation of Türkiye's security policies in the fight against terrorism will be analyzed. The increase in the activities of terrorist groups worldwide and the emergence of more porous borders have forced governments to transform their security policies and counter-terrorism methods. Türkiye has employed various counter-terrorism methods against the Partiya Karkeren Kurdistane (PKK) since its first attack in Eruh in 1984. In the 1990s, Türkiye used mostly military counter-terrorism methods in its fight against the PKK. However, between 2002 and 2015, Türkiye has prioritized democratic norms and negotiation methods in its attitude towards the PKK. This article analyses the reasons for this transformation.
